text.title: Breaking Change Deprecation Policy Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules for the one policy that decides what counts as a breaking change to a design-system component or token, how long the deprecation window runs, and what must be true before removal executes. Governance (the umbrella operating model) references this policy; it does not restate it.

rule.statement: The policy MUST enumerate what forces a MAJOR bump, as a closed list: removing or renaming a component, a prop, or a token key; changing a prop's default value; changing a token's type (dimension → string, colour → alias); removing a DOM element, slot, or class name that consumers style; tightening a prop's accepted value set. Everything not on the list is MINOR (additive) or PATCH. An unclassified change MUST NOT be published.

rationale.source: Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 §8 + W3C Design Tokens Format Module

rule.rationale: Consumers pin with caret ranges, so anything published below MAJOR lands in every consumer's next install without a human reading the diff. A token key rename shipped as PATCH resolves to `undefined` at build time in every consumer simultaneously — classification is the only gate between the change and that fan-out.

rule.statement: Any token value change that moves a documented foreground/background pairing below WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 (4.5:1 body text, 3:1 large text) or SC 1.4.11 (3:1 for UI component and graphical boundaries) is MAJOR regardless of how similar it looks. The policy records the before and after ratio for every affected pairing.
rule.rationale: Colour tweaks ship as PATCH because they "look the same", but contrast is not linear in perceptual similarity — a 2% lightness shift can cross 4.5:1. The change is invisible in review and turns every consumer surface using that pairing into an audit finding at once, with no code change on the consumer side to point at.

rule.statement: `deprecation_window_days` MUST be at least two release cycles of the slowest consumer named in `consumer_teams`. For native app consumers the cycle is measured against forced-update or version-adoption data, not against store submission date. The policy states which consumer set the floor.

rationale.source: Angular Deprecation Practices (deprecated APIs supported for two major versions, ~12 months)

rule.rationale: A web consumer redeploys the day the fix lands; a native binary already on devices keeps calling the old component for the whole adoption tail. A window computed off web cadence expires while shipped builds still depend on the removed API, and those builds cannot be patched — only re-released and re-adopted.

rule.statement: If the change is mechanically migratable (symbol rename, prop signature change, token key rename), a codemod MUST ship in the same release as the deprecation notice — jscodeshift/ts-morph for component APIs, a Style Dictionary alias or token-key map for tokens. Without a published, runnable codemod, `removal_date` extends by one additional full consumer release cycle.

rationale.source: React and MUI v4→v5 codemod-led migration practice

rule.rationale: A rename touching hundreds of call-sites becomes manual work each consumer must schedule, and manual migration work always loses prioritisation to feature work. The window then expires with usage unchanged, which forces either a broken removal or an indefinite extension — the codemod is what converts the migration from a planning problem to a command.

rule.statement: Through the whole window the deprecated API MUST stay functional and emit exactly one warning per deprecated symbol per session, in development builds only, naming the replacement, the `removal_date`, and the `migration_guide_ref` URL. Warnings on every render, or warnings present in production bundles, violate the rule.

rationale.source: Node.js runtime deprecation model (DEP codes, --pending-deprecation) and React dev-only warnings

rule.rationale: Per-render warnings flood the console within seconds, so consumer teams add a blanket console filter — and the filter suppresses the one deprecation that mattered along with the noise. Once-per-symbol keeps the signal above the team's tolerance threshold for the full window.

rule.statement: Removal executes only when a static scan across consumer repositories reports zero remaining imports or token references, with the scan command, the date, and the repository list attached as evidence. Self-reported "we're migrated" from a consumer team is not evidence.

rationale.source: ESLint no-restricted-imports rules plus component-usage analytics (Omlet, Figma library analytics)

rule.rationale: Teams report migration status per their own tracking ticket, which closes when the primary surface is done and leaves the long tail — tests, storybook stories, internal admin screens — still importing. The scan finds those; the ticket does not, and the removal breaks a surface nobody remembered owning.

rule.statement: Do NOT apply when (a) the component or token has no consumer outside the repository that owns it — an atomic rename in a single PR needs no window, (b) the system is pre-1.0 with a published "API unstable" contract, (c) nothing is versioned or tagged, so there is no prior version for consumers to remain on. In (c) route to design-system-governance to establish versioning first.

rationale.source: Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 §4 (0.y.z carries no stability guarantee)

rule.rationale: A deprecation window is a promise about a published version. Without a published version there is nothing to deprecate against, and the policy's timeline fields become dates nobody can act on.
